'''''Psidium cattleyanum''''' (World Plants: ''Psidium cattleianum''),<ref name=GRIN>{{cite web|last=USDA-ARS|title=GRIN Taxonomy for Plants|url=https://npgsweb.ars-grin.gov/gringlobal/taxonomydetail.aspx?id=30200 |access-date=6 May 2016}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|last=Missouri Botanical Gardens|title=Tropicos.org|url=http://www.tropicos.org/Name/22102275?tab=acceptednames|access-date=9 June 2011}}</ref> commonly known as '''Cattley guava''', '''strawberry guava''' or '''cherry guava''', is a small tree ({{cvt|2|–|6|m|0}} tall) in the [[Myrtaceae]] (myrtle) family. The species is named in honour of English horticulturist [[William Cattley]]. The red-fruited variety, ''P. cattleyanum var. cattleyanum'', is commonly known as purple guava, '''red cattley guava''', red strawberry guava and red cherry guava.<ref name=GRIN/> The yellow-fruited variety, ''P. cattleyanum'' var. ''littorale'' is variously known as '''yellow cattley guava''', yellow strawberry guava, yellow cherry guava,<ref name=GRIN/> lemon guava and in [[Hawaii]] as ''waiawī''.

It is an [[invasive plant]] in many areas and is considered the most invasive species in Hawaii, although it has some economic uses, including its edible fruit.

== Description ==
''Psidium cattleyanum'' is a small, highly branched tree that reaches a maximum height of {{cvt|13|m|0}}, although most individuals are between {{cvt|2|and(-)|4|m|0}}.<ref name=":2">{{Cite web|url=http://eol.org/pages/2508592/overview|title=Strawberry Guava - Psidium cattleianum - Overview - Encyclopedia of Life|website=Encyclopedia of Life|language=en|access-date=2017-05-06}}</ref> It has smooth, grey to reddish-brown bark, with oval to elliptical leaves that grow to 4.5 cm in length. It bears fruit when the plants are between 3 and 6 years old. This fruit has thin skin that ranges from yellow to a dark red or purple, is ovular in shape, and grows to around 4 cm in length. Its flowers grow either individually or in clusters of three, and each flower has five petals.<ref name=":2" />

''P. cattleyanum'' reproduces through setting seed and through cloning. Clonally produced suckers tend to have a greater leaf area.<ref name=":5">Huenneke, L. (1990). Seedling and clonal recruitment of the invasive tree Psidium cattleianum: Implications for management of native Hawaiian forests. ''Biological Conservation'' 53(3): 199–211.</ref>

''P. cattleyanum'' is in the [[Hardiness zone|USDA hardiness zones]] 9a–11.<ref>{{cite web|title=Psidium cattleianum|website=Florida Natural Areas Inventory|date=13 June 2017|url=https://www.fnai.org/species-communities/invasives/invasive-species?ID=130|access-date=5 March 2025}} </ref>

== Etymology ==
The genus name, ''Psidium'', comes from the Latin ''psidion'' ('armlet').<ref>{{Cite web |title=Definition of PSIDIUM |url=https://www.merriam-webster.com/dictionary/Psidium |access-date=2017-05-04 |website=www.merriam-webster.com |language=en}}</ref>

== Distribution ==
Though native to Brazil, it is now distributed throughout many tropical regions.<ref name=":0">US Forest Service. (2016). Strawberry Guava: Not All Green Is Good. Pacific Southwest Research Station.</ref><ref name=":1">Lowe S., Browne M., Boudjelas S., De Poorter M. (2000) ''100 of the World’s Worst Invasive Alien Species: A selection from the Global Invasive Species Database''. Published by The Invasive Species Specialist Group (ISSG) a specialist group of the Species Survival Commission (SSC) of the World Conservation Union (IUCN), 1
pp. First published as special lift-out in Aliens 12, December 2000. Updated and reprinted version: November 2004.</ref> It was introduced in [[Hawaii]] as early as 1825 to create an agricultural market for its fruits, but it has yet to be a commercially viable product. It is now highly prevalent in tropical rainforest ecosystems due mainly to accidental transportation and its [[Invasive species|invasive]] plant properties.<ref name=":0" /><ref name=":9">C. Wikler, J. Pedrosa-Macedo, M. Vitorino, M. Caxambú, C. Smith. (1999). Strawberry Guava (Psidium cattleianum) – Prospects for Biological Control. ''Proceedings of the X International Symposium on Biological Control of Weeds'' 4–14 July 1999. Montana State University, Bozeman, Montana. Edited by Neal R. Spencer pp. 659-665 (2000).</ref>

== Ecology ==
''P. cattleyanum'' occurs primarily in mesic [[tropical rainforest]] environments<ref name=":5" /> at an elevation of up to {{cvt|1300|m|ft}}, but is found primarily below {{cvt|800|m|ft}}.<ref name=":6">Smith, C. W. 1985. Impact of alien plants on Hawaii's native biota. pp. 180-250. in C. P. Stone and J. M. Scott (eds.). Hawaii's terrestrial ecosystems: preservation and management. Univ. Hawaii Coop. Natl. Park Resour. Studies Unit, University of Hawaii Press. pp. 584.</ref> Its native range is restricted to the Amazonian Basin in Brazil, but it has established in many other tropical areas of similar characteristics.<ref name=":4">{{Cite web |title=Strawberry Guava - Psidium cattleianum - Overview - Encyclopedia of Life |url=http://eol.org/pages/2508592/overview |access-date=2017-05-04 |website=Encyclopedia of Life |language=en}}</ref><ref name=":5" />

''P. cattleyanum'' does not dominate plant communities in its native range.<ref name=":0" /> It is considered invasive due to its robust tolerance to many different environments.<ref name=":7">{{Cite web|url=http://eol.org/pages/2508592/details#habitat|title=Strawberry Guava - Psidium cattleianum - Details - Encyclopedia of Life|website=Encyclopedia of Life|language=en|access-date=2017-05-06}}</ref> ''P. cattleyanum'' is prevalent in both undisturbed<ref name=":5" /> and highly disturbed roadside habitats in its invasive range.<ref name=":6" /> Its invasive quality may be explained by a high amount of genetic variation, as variants of different fruit colors cluster at different elevations.<ref name=":8">Huenneke, L.F. and P. M. Vitousek. 1989. Seedling and clonal recruitment of the invasive tree Psidium cattleianum: implications for management of native Hawaiian forests. ''Biological Conservation'' 53: 199-211.</ref> Additionally, ''P. cattleyanum'' is both very shade-tolerant<ref name=":6" /> and able to withstand soils with a moderate to high pH level.<ref>Sem, G. S. 1984. A population study and distribution of strawberry guava (Psidium cattleianum) in Hawaii Volcanoes National Park, Hawaii. Master's thesis. Univ. Hawaii, Honolulu. 84 pp.</ref> It is also capable of withstanding heavy [[leaf litter]] and responding to bending or breaking of its branches by generating vigorous shoots.<ref name=":8" />

''P. cattleyanum'' is often associated with invasive feral pigs<ref name=":5" /><ref name=":7" /> The two species are often found near each other, most likely because feral pigs aid in the spread of ''P. cattleyanum''. The pigs disturb habitats by digging in the soil, making it easier for ''P. cattleyanum'' seeds to reach the soil. Additionally, feral pigs may ingest the fruits, whose seeds reach the soil in the scat of the feral pigs.<ref name=":5" />

Preliminary research suggests that ''P. cattleyanum'' is [[Allelopathy|allelopathic]],<ref name=":6" /> as its roots have been found to inhibit the growth of at least two other plant species when [[soil pH]] was not a factor.<ref name=":10">Brown, R. L., C. S. Tang, and R. K. Nishimoto. 1983. Growth inhibition from guava root exudates. ''HortScience'' 13(3): 316-318.</ref>

=== As an invasive species ===
[[File:Starr 040518-0060 Psidium cattleianum.jpg|thumb|220px|Invasive growth in Hawaii]]
Native to [[Brazil]]—where it is known as ''araçá''—and adjacent tropical South America, ''P. cattleyanum'' is closely related to [[Psidium guajava|common guava]] (''P. guajava''). Like that species, it is a widespread, highly invasive species in tropical areas throughout the Indian and Pacific Oceans.<ref name=":4" />

It was introduced to many of the areas it now invades due to human usage as a crop for its edible fruit.<ref name=":1" /> It is considered the most invasive plant in Hawaii.<ref name=":4" /><ref name=":1" /> It is also among the most invasive species on [[Réunion]] and Madagascar,<ref> https://www.eurekalert.org/news-releases/1116248</ref> where it poses a significant threat to the endemic forests. It has also spread to the [[Azores]], though it is not as invasive there.<ref>{{cite web|last1=Reis|first1=Júlio Gaspar|title=Lista de taxa invasores e de risco para Portugal|url=https://arocha.pt/wp-content/uploads/2018/02/taxa-invasores-risco-0-1.pdf|access-date=19 August 2021|page=78|lang=pt}}</ref> It is sporadically [[Naturalisation (biology)|naturalised]] in coastal areas of Queensland and northern New South Wales. It is also naturalised on Lord Howe Island, Norfolk Island and Christmas Island (Navie 2004; Queensland Herbarium 2008).

The species is able to propagate quickly due to the spread of its fruit and seeds, which is facilitated by birds and [[feral pig]]s,<ref name=":5" /> as well as through its root sprouts. The yellow variety bears more heavily than the red and generally has larger fruit.<ref>{{cite web|title=Psidium Cattleyanum|url=http://www.environment.gov.au/cgi-bin/biodiversity/invasive/weeds/weeddetails.pl?taxon_id=5397|website=Weeds in Australia|publisher=Department of the Environment, The Australian Government|access-date=3 August 2015}}</ref> It tends to form dense, monotypic thickets that block sunlight and prevent the growth of native species,<ref name=":11">{{Cite web|url=https://www.nps.gov/plants/alien/fact/psca1.htm|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/19990508011253/http://www.nps.gov/plants/alien/fact/psca1.htm|url-status=dead|archive-date=May 8, 1999|title=PCA Alien Plant Working Group - Strawberry Guava (Psidium cattleianum)|last=PCA/APWG|website=www.nps.gov|access-date=2017-05-07}}</ref> and is very difficult to eradicate. It also provides refuge for fruit flies, which cause extensive agricultural damage.<ref name="Biological Control of Strawberry Guava in Hawaii">{{cite web|last=US Forest Service, Institute of Pacific Islands Forestry|title=Biological Control of Strawberry Guava in Hawaii|url=http://www.fs.fed.us/psw/programs/ipif/strawberryguava/|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20090403112828/http://www.fs.fed.us/psw/programs/ipif/strawberryguava/|url-status=dead|archive-date=3 April 2009|access-date=29 June 2012}}</ref>

''P. cattleyanum'' grows effectively in undisturbed areas,<ref name=":5" /> complicating restoration efforts in sensitive habitats. Its presence in damaged ecosystems further complicates management due to its high dispersal from these less-sensitive habitats to more fragile habitats.<ref name=":8" /> Its ability to thrive in a variety of different habitats under many different ecological conditions<ref name=":8" /> threatens native flora of many different habitat types.<ref name=":11" /> Additionally, its potential [[Allelopathy|allelopathic]] qualities<ref name=":6" /> further complicate the ability of other plant species to coexist.<ref name=":10" />

==== Control strategies ====
[[File:Starr 041113-0636 Psidium cattleianum.jpg|thumb|right|220px|Dense thicket growth in Hawaii forests]]
A variety of management strategies have been applied to ''P. cattleyanum'' management efforts due to its ubiquity and the various ways it spreads.<ref name=":9" /> Despite the great threat that ''P. cattleyanum'' poses to many tropical ecosystems, some studies indicate that isolated groups can be totally eradicated after three to four years of proper management applications, such as cutting and burning mature individuals and applying herbicide to stumps.<ref name=":3">Tunison, J. T., & Stone, C. P. (1992). [http://manoa.hawaii.edu/hpicesu/book/1992_chap/41.pdf Special ecological areas: an approach to alien plant control in Hawaii Volcanoes National Park.] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20111025115622/http://manoa.hawaii.edu/hpicesu/book/1992_chap/41.pdf |date=2011-10-25 }} Alien plant invasions in native ecosystems of Hawaii. ''Hawai'i: management and research'', 781-798.</ref> However, continued follow-up management is necessary indefinitely after a period of high-intensity restoration.<ref name=":3" /> This management strategy, known as the “special ecological areas,” is one of the strongest ways of controlling plant species over time.<ref name=":3" /> It works by focusing wood removal, burning, and other management efforts in the designated efforts.<ref name=":3" />

Feral pigs and non-native birds contribute to the spread of ''P. cattleyanum'' via seed dispersal. Thus, some control efforts involve removal and control of invasive fauna.<ref name=":5" /> However, results from such efforts are often unsuccessful due to the lack of dependence upon the animals for dispersal, as [[germination]] occurs under a wide variety of conditions.<ref name=":5" />

Another management technique is the introduction of insects that act as parasites on the invasive plants.<ref name=":9" /> This biological control approach is used because certain insects cause damage to ''P. cattleyanum'' in a way that either prevents the tree from reproducing or kills them outright. Most of the proposed insects infect the tree with bud or leaf galls, effectively preventing fruit growth or photosynthesis.<ref name=":9" /> For example, ''[[Dasineura]] gigantea'' caused bud galls that inhibited shoot growth.<ref name=":9" /> The [[Tectococcus ovatus|Brazilian Scale]] is a potential [[biological control]] agent used in [[Florida]],<ref name="wesselsetal2007">Wessels, Frank J., James P. Cuda, M. Tracy Johnson and José Henrique Pedrosa-Macedo. 2007. [https://doi.org/10.1007%2Fs10526-006-9043-3 Host specificity of Tectococcus ovatus (Hemiptera: Eriococcidae), a potential biological control agent of the invasive strawberry guava, Psidium cattleianum (Myrtales: Myrtaceae), in Florida.]  BioControl. Volume 52, Number 4 / August, 2007.</ref> and [[Hawaii]].<ref name="strawberryguavabiocontroldotorg">{{cite web|url= http://www.hear.org/strawberryguavabiocontrol/|title= Strawberry Guava Biocontrol: Restoring natural balance to Hawaii's forests and watersheds with the help of a bug|date=23 June 2010|work=Hawaiian Ecosystems at Risk project}}</ref> However, some insects cannot be used due to the potential for certain species to attack more than ''P. cattleyanum''.<ref name=":9" /> One such species, the [[sawfly]] (''Haplostegus epimelas''), attacked commercially produced guava plants in addition to invasive ''P. cattleyanum''.<ref name=":9" />

==Uses==
Both the fruit's thin skin and juicy interior are soft and edible. It can also be used to make jam and juices. The skin is often removed for a sweeter flavour. The seeds are small and white in colour. Its leaves may be brewed for tea.<ref>{{Cite news|url=http://www.eattheweeds.com/psidium-littorale-var-cattleianumstrawberry-guava-2/|title=Strawberry Guava|work=Eat The Weeds and other things, too|access-date=2017-05-07|language=en-US}}</ref> The wood of the tree is hard, compact, durable, and resistant, and is used for lathe work, tool handles, charcoal, and firewood. The plant is indispensable for mixed planting in reforestation of reclaimed and protected areas in Brazil.<ref>{{cite book |title= Edible Medicinal And Non Medicinal Plants: Volume 3, Fruits |volume= 3 |author= Lim T. K. |edition= illustrated |publisher= Springer Science & Business Media |year= 2012 |isbn= 9789400725348 |page= 677}}</ref>

''P. cattleyanum'' has modest economic impacts in Hawaii due to its edible fruits.<ref name="GRIN" /><ref name=":0" /><ref name=":3" /><ref>State of Hawaii. (2010). Biocontrol of Strawberry Guava by its Natural Control Agent for Preservation of Native Forests in the Hawaiian Islands. Department of Land and Natural Resources, 54.</ref> However, products made from ''P. cattleyanum'' are not commercially available because of a lack of market and the heavy presence of fruit flies. This renders the fruits inedible soon after they are picked.<ref name=":3" /> Its seeds have many health benefits, including antioxidant, anti-inflammatory, and antimicrobial properties in addition to a high amount of vitamin C.<ref name=":2" /><ref>K. McCook-Russell, M. Nair, P. Facey, C. Bowen-Forbes. (2012). [http://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0308814612004785 Nutritional and nutraceutical comparison of Jamaican Psidium cattleianum (strawberry guava) and Psidium guajava (common guava) fruits.] ''Food Chemistry'' 134(2): 1069–1073.</ref>

Necklaces are reported to be handcrafted in Tanzania by tying together beads made of individual fruits.<ref>{{cite web |url= https://www.botanicalbeads.com |title= Botanical Beads of the World |last= Smith |first= Ruth J. |date= 2005 |website= |publisher= University of California, Santa Barbara |access-date= 11 August 2023 |quote=}}</ref>
